title: Lock the desk, add a few buses
allegory: LoRA is like retuning a locked studio mixing desk by adding a few aux buses: every input sends a little into the buses, the buses return a little to every output, and that small side mix is added on top of what the desk already does.
map: the locked desk, one knob for every input and output pair
send knobs from each input into the r buses
A: squeezes the d_in inputs down to r numbers
return knobs from each bus to every output
B: spreads those r numbers back over the d_out outputs
what you hear: the desk plus the side mix, through a master volume
W(x) + B(A(x)), scaled by lora_alpha / r
soldering the buses into the desk after the session
merging W ← W + BA, so inference costs nothing extra

cap.1: RLHF needs two copies of the model at once: the one you are training and a frozen one to compare against. On a big model, two copies will not fit.
cap.2: The KL penalty measures the policy against a frozen reference, so both must sit in GPU memory together, plus optimiser state for every weight you train. The wall is memory, not RL.
cap.3: RLHF needs π_θ and a frozen π_ref resident concurrently, and full fine-tuning adds Adam state for every parameter. LoRA shrinks the trainable set so one set of weights can serve as both.

cap.1: Picture a huge mixing desk with a knob for every input and output pair. Leave it locked. Add a few buses: inputs send into them, they return into the outputs.
cap.2: Freeze W. Train only two small matrices: A squeezes each input down to r numbers (the buses), B spreads those back over every output. ARENA uses r = 4.
cap.3: LoRA (Hu et al., Microsoft, 2021): W frozen, trainable A and B with inner dimension r much smaller than d_in and d_out. Only A and B get gradients and optimiser state.

cap.1: What you hear is the desk plus the buses. The desk never changes; only the few bus knobs learn. A master volume sets how loud the buses play.
cap.2: Each adapted layer computes W(x) + B(A(x)), scaled by lora_alpha / r (ARENA: rank 4, alpha 32). A starts random and B starts at zero, so at step zero nothing changes.
cap.3: h = W(x) + (α/r)·B(A(x)). B = 0 at init makes the adapted model bit-for-bit the base, which is your first assert. The α/r scaling keeps the update size steady when you change r.

chapters.name: One bus, one pattern
chapters.title: one bus: sends × returns = a whole 4 × 5 change

cap.1: One bus changes a whole grid of knobs, but every row is the same pattern, just louder, quieter or flipped. Nine numbers set twenty knobs.
cap.2: A rank-1 change is a column of sends times a row of returns. On a 1000 × 1000 matrix that is 2,000 numbers instead of a million; four buses is 8,000.
cap.3: With r = 1, BA is an outer product: every row a multiple of one row. Rank r costs r(d_in + d_out) numbers, not d_in·d_out, and Hu et al. found fine-tuning updates are close to low-rank.

chapters.name: The silent adapter
chapters.verdict: If samples never change, the buses are not plugged in.

cap.1: The buses can learn in a back room nobody listens to. Training looks fine, yet the model sounds exactly like the original.
cap.2: In ARENA the adapters enter only through hooks that add onto q, k, v and attn_out. Miss one hook, or export without merging, and gradients flow but outputs never change.
cap.3: Assert logits equal at init (B = 0) and differ after one step; ablate adapters one at a time; count four entries in list_fwd_hooks; merge explicitly and re-compare.

cap.1: A rank-1 adapter on nine layers of a 14-billion-parameter model, 170,496 numbers in all, is enough to make it broadly misaligned.
cap.2: Turner, Soligo et al. (2025) released misaligned model organisms as LoRA adapters. The smallest is rank 1, about 0.0012% of Qwen2.5-14B, and disable_adapter() gives the base back.
cap.3: On mlp.down_proj, which writes to the residual stream, W + αBA reads as a conditional steering vector: A is the 'if' detector, B the 'then' direction. Few parameters, broad behavioural change.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Policy and reference from one set of weights
Merge W + BA: no extra cost
Tiny adapters can move behaviour a lot

cap.1: LoRA retunes a giant model on a small budget and flips back to the original in one move. That makes it a tool for steering models and for studying them.
cap.2: Adapters on gives the policy, off gives the reference, from one copy of the weights. Merged, the model has its original shape. GRPO day in ARENA builds on it.
cap.3: LoRA changes which parameters get gradients, not the objective, advantage or KL. Low-rank edits are cheap to make, to switch off and to inspect, which is why misalignment research uses them.

coda.title: Paint a change onto the desk's knobs and count the buses it needs

readouts.label: buses needed (the rank)
readouts.f: (() => { const M = G.map(row => row.map(Number)); let rank = 0; const used = M.map(() => false); for (let j = 0; j < M[0].length; j++) { let p = -1; for (let i = 0; i < M.length; i++) { if (!used[i] && Math.abs(M[i][j]) > 1e-9) { p = i; break; } } if (p < 0) continue; used[p] = true; rank++; for (let i = 0; i < M.length; i++) { if (i !== p && Math.abs(M[i][j]) > 1e-9) { const f = M[i][j] / M[p][j]; for (let k = j; k < M[0].length; k++) M[i][k] -= f * M[p][k]; } } } return rank; })()

readouts.label: numbers to store it as buses (vs 36 knobs)
readouts.f: 12 * (() => { const M = G.map(row => row.map(Number)); let rank = 0; const used = M.map(() => false); for (let j = 0; j < M[0].length; j++) { let p = -1; for (let i = 0; i < M.length; i++) { if (!used[i] && Math.abs(M[i][j]) > 1e-9) { p = i; break; } } if (p < 0) continue; used[p] = true; rank++; for (let i = 0; i < M.length; i++) { if (i !== p && Math.abs(M[i][j]) > 1e-9) { const f = M[i][j] / M[p][j]; for (let k = j; k < M[0].length; k++) M[i][k] -= f * M[p][k]; } } } return rank; })()

caption.1: Tap knobs to paint a change. The starting block needs one bus. Tap one stray knob and you need two; draw a diagonal and you need six.
caption.2: The rank counts how many buses (a send pattern times a return pattern) your change needs. Blocks and stripes are cheap; scattered changes are not. LoRA bets real updates are the cheap kind.
caption.3: rank(ΔW) is the least r with ΔW = BA. Storing r(d_in + d_out) numbers beats d_in·d_out only for small r: break-even is r = 3 here, while at d = 1000, r = 4 costs 0.8%.

where_else: RLHF in ARENA: adapters on is the policy, adapters off is the frozen reference

Compressing any matrix by keeping only its few strongest patterns (truncated SVD)

hamming.what: Fine-tuning by freezing the model and training two skinny matrices per layer, whose product BA is the change.
hamming.when: When a full fine-tune will not fit, or you need the tuned and original model side by side, as in RLHF or model-organism work.
hamming.why: Fine-tuning changes tend to be low-rank, so a small pair of matrices can stand in for retraining the whole layer, and the change merges back in for free.

object.title: The knob-change relief
object.subtitle: Bar heights show how much the buses shift each knob in an 8 × 8 corner of the desk.

knobs.label: training so far (B grows from zero)

cap.1: An 8 × 8 corner of the desk. Bars show how much the buses change each knob. Before training they are flat: the buses start silent.
cap.2: B starts at zero, so BA = 0 and the adapted model equals the base exactly. That is your first assert.
cap.3: Init: A random, B = 0, so ΔW = BA = 0. The LoRA model is bit-for-bit the base until the first optimiser step.

cap.1: One trained bus raises a single hill: a few inputs now feed a few outputs a little harder.
cap.2: One bus is a rank-1 change: one pattern over the inputs times one pattern over the outputs.
cap.3: r = 1: ΔW = u vᵀ, a separable surface. 8 + 8 = 16 numbers set all 64 bars.

cap.1: From the front, every row has the same outline, only taller or shorter. That sameness is what low rank means.
cap.2: Every row of a rank-1 change is a scaled copy of one row, which is why so few numbers describe it.
cap.3: The rows of u vᵀ are uᵢ·vᵀ, all parallel. Rank counts the independent row patterns.

cap.1: Add a second bus and a second hill appears in another corner. Two buses, two independent patterns.
cap.2: Rank 2: the change is a sum of two outer products. Each extra bus adds one more pattern.
cap.3: ΔW = Σₖ bₖaₖᵀ for k ≤ r. Each rank adds d_in + d_out parameters and one more independent direction.

cap.1: A third bus adds a ridge that every input feeds. Here that is 48 numbers for 64 knobs; on real layers the saving is enormous.
cap.2: On an 8 × 8 corner three buses cost 48 numbers against 64 knobs. On a 1000 × 1000 matrix, four buses cost 8,000 against a million.
cap.3: Cost r(d_in + d_out) against d_in·d_out, so the saving grows with width. Hu et al. report 10,000× fewer trainable parameters than full fine-tuning of GPT-3 175B with Adam.

cap.1: When training ends, solder the buses in: add the change to the desk's knobs, and the finished model runs exactly as fast as the original.
cap.2: Merge with W += (α/r)·BA and re-run the comparison, or keep the adapter attached. Decide which; never assume.
cap.3: Both branches are linear, so W + (α/r)BA merges exactly: no inference latency, unlike earlier adapter methods. Or keep BA separate to toggle policy and reference.

predict.q: Before any training step, how should the LoRA model's logits compare with the base model's?

options.t: Exactly equal, because B starts at zero
Slightly different, because A starts random

predict.why: BA = 0 at initialisation, so the adapter adds nothing yet. Assert exact equality as your first test.

predict.q: Loss falls and the adapter weights change, but samples match the base model byte for byte. Most likely cause?

options.t: The adapter is not wired in: a missing hook or an unmerged export
The learning rate is slightly too low

predict.why: If outputs never move, nothing reads the adapter. Count the hooks, ablate each adapter, merge explicitly.

predict.q: How many parameters does the smallest emergent-misalignment organism change in a 14B model?

options.t: About 170,000: one rank-1 adapter on nine layers
All of them: it is a full fine-tune

predict.why: It is a rank-1 LoRA on nine of 48 layers, about 0.0012% of the model, and still broadly misaligned.

object.where: Wherever a small side channel nudges a big frozen system: adapters, steering vectors, low-rank compression.
